Learning Objectives
Describe relevant pediatric foot and ankle anatomy.

Many injuries often are successfully managed nonsurgically.
Normal ossification variants, apophyses, and varying physeal morphology make radiographic
diagnosis of injuries a challenge in growing athletes.

Overview
Foot and ankle injuries in pediatric patients are common. Most are successfully managed
nonsurgically, including via immobilization, weight-bearing modifications, and physical
therapy. Orthopaedic surgeons should be able to distinguish normal osseous anatomy
from acute injuries in this growing patient population.
Epidemiology
10% of all fractures in children occur in the foot and ankle.
Salter-Harris type I and type II fractures account for 90% of isolated distal fibula fractures.
Based on MRIs, ankle sprains are more common than Salter-Harris type I distal fibula
fractures.1,2

Epidemiology
Foot and ankle fractures are common in pediatric patients, accounting for a combined
10% of pediatric fractures and almost 20% of physeal injuries. Salter-Harris type I and
type II distal fibula fractures account for 90% of isolated distal fibula fractures.
Nondisplaced Salter-Harris type I distal fibula fractures are diagnosed based on clinical
examination (point tenderness over the physis) if radiographic findings are normal.
These injuries are at risk for over-management (eg, management of lateral ankle
ligament injuries as physeal fractures).3,4 MRIs of acute lateral ankle injuries in pediatric
patients have shown that most are ligamentous injuries without substantial pathology at
the distal fibula physis.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Knowledge of the locations of the physes, apophyses, and accessory ossification centers is
paramount to understanding injuries and fractures versus normal anatomy.
The lateral ankle ligament complex is intimately associated with the distal fibula physis.
Peroneal tendons traverse posterior to the distal fibula and its physis, limiting reconstruction
options.
Osteology
The location of the physis varies between the first metatarsal and the second through fifth
metatarsals.
Accessory ossification centers are common in skeletally immature patients.

Osteology
Numerous accessory ossification centers around the foot and ankle must be
distinguished from fractures5 (Figure 1; Resource 1). The distal fibular epiphysis ossific
nucleus begins ossification in children aged 18 to 20 months and may have an accessory
ossification center called the os fibulare at its most distal extent. Other important
accessory ossification centers to recognize are the os vesalianum at the base of the fifth
metatarsal and the os sustentaculum inferior to the medial malleolus, which should not
be confused with fractures or avulsions. The base of the fifth metatarsal has an
apophysis (accessory ossification center) near the attachment of the peroneus brevis
tendon that may be confused with avulsions by surgeons unfamiliar with this unique
bone anatomy6 (Figure 2; Resource 2).
Metatarsal physes are present at the base of the first metatarsal and the heads of the
second through fifth metatarsals7 (Figure 3; Resource 3).

Tendons
The relationship of tendon insertions to physes and apophyses is important in guiding the
diagnosis and management of pediatric foot and ankle injuries.

Tendons
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Foot and Ankle Sports Injuries in Pediatric Patients
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002083
5/34

The peroneus longus and brevis tendons wrap around the lateral malleolus and are held
in place by the osseous constraint of the distal fibula and the soft-tissue restraint of the
superior peroneal retinaculum. The peroneus brevis tendon attaches onto the base of
the fifth metatarsal and may result in avulsion fractures in inversion injuries. The tibialis
posterior tendon attaches to the medial navicular and accessory navicular, if present.
Joints and Ligaments
The proximity of lateral ankle ligaments to the distal fibular physis means that diagnosis of
lateral ankle injuries is based on the anatomic location of the point tenderness on
examination.

Joints and Ligaments
The ankle is a hinge joint with stability provided by its articular congruity and
surrounding ligamentous attachments. The medial deltoid originates on the medial
malleolus of the distal tibia, inserting onto the talus (deep and superficial deltoid),
calcaneus (superficial deltoid only), and navicular (superficial deltoid only). The lateral
ankle ligaments, which include the anterior talofibular ligament, calcaneofibular
ligament, and posterior talofibular ligament, originate on the distal fibula near the distal
fibular physis. The interosseous membrane and the anterior and posterior inferior
tibiofibular ligaments make up the syndesmosis, with the anterior and posterior inferior
tibiofibular ligaments inserting onto the distal tibia epiphysis.
Etiology and Mechanism of Injury
Low-energy injuries (acute inversion or overuse) are more common in youth sports, with
higher-energy mechanisms resulting in more substantial injuries.

Etiology and Mechanism of Injury

In young athletes, low-energy lateral ankle injuries consisting of an inversion event are
relatively common. Higher-energy mechanisms of injury include falls from bikes,
scooters, or playground equipment; motor vehicle collisions; etc. and may lead to
increasing severity of foot and ankle pathology.
Risk Factors
Growth rate, joint mobility, sport played, and injury history are risk factors.
Ligamentous laxity, previous injury, altered proprioception, and functional movement abilities
(eg, presence of tarsal coalition) are risk factors for pediatric foot and ankle injuries.
During periods of rapid growth, injury rates can increase and are attributed to variations in
hormones, sensitivity of physes to injury, and lack of motor coordination.
Associated Injuries
Neurovascular injuries and compartment syndromes are exceedingly rare with pediatric foot
and ankle injuries.
Regardless, a thorough physical examination should include evaluation and documentation of
neurovascular status.
Injury Classification
Use pediatric-specific injury classification systems in describing injuries or fractures.
The Salter-Harris classification system is routinely used to describe foot and ankle fractures
(Figure 4).
Fractures of the base of the fifth metatarsal are routinely described based on the type of injury
(Table 1).

Figure 4 Illustration shows the Salter-Harris classification of foot and ankle fractures. Type I is
characterized by physeal separation. Type II is characterized by a fracture line that extends
transversely through the physis and exits through the metaphysis. Type III is characterized by a
fracture that traverses the physis and exits through the epiphysis. Type IV is characterized by a
fracture line that passes through the epiphysis, across the physis, and out the metaphysis. Type V
is a crush injury to the physis. (Reproduced from Kay RM, Matthys GA: Pediatric ankle fractures:
Evaluation and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2001;9[4]:268-278.)

Patient History
Typically, an acute injury; determine ability to bear weight

Patient History
First metatarsal fractures account for a large percentage of tarsal and metatarsal
injuries in children, and they are more commonly observed in children younger than 5
years. Direct or indirect mechanisms of injury (axial load, inversion, and/or rotation)
may cause these injuries. If the injury occurs proximally at the base of the metatarsal,
evaluation of the tarsometatarsal joint for concomitant injury is paramount. Weight-
bearing radiographs can be used to evaluate for soft-tissue injuries in these
situations. If the normal relationships among osseous structures are noted to be
disrupted on weight-bearing radiographs, suspicion of a soft-tissue or ligamentous
injury should be increased; however, Lisfranc injuries are rare in children.
Physical Examination
Palpation and assessment of unique pediatric anatomy will help define injuries.

Physical Examination
Assess the location of swelling, ecchymosis, and tenderness to palpation. Ensure
palpation specifically over the physes; apophyses; and surrounding soft tissues,
including ligament and tendon insertions and the interosseous space. Assess joint
range of motion and stability and the joint proximal and distal to the site of suspected
injury.
Neurovascular Examination
A standard neurovascular examination (including palpation of pulses and sensorimotor
evaluation) is warranted, with consideration of progressive neurologic conditions that may
manifest as medial foot pathology in childhood (eg, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease).


Neurovascular Examination
Patients with multiple metatarsal fractures, midfoot ligamentous injuries, or high-
energy mechanisms of injury should be evaluated for compartment syndromes and
treated appropriately.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Weight-bearing radiographs, if possible, will help define pathology.

Radiography
Three-view foot radiographs (AP, lateral, and oblique) are warranted for work up of
pediatric foot injuries. In an acute setting, supine, non–weight-bearing radiographs
are the standard of care. Weight-bearing radiographs may be useful in evaluating foot
soft-tissue injuries and deformities. Stress radiographs rarely are indicated in this
patient population unless concern for ligamentous Lisfranc injuries exists.
Computed Tomography
Rarely indicated for fracture pattern or description
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Rarely indicated unless concern for ligamentous Lisfranc injury exists and the child is unable to
bear weight for stress radiography
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications

Most patients are successfully treated nonsurgically via weight bearing as tolerated in a short
leg walking cast or cast shoe.
Contraindications
Multiple displaced metatarsal fractures or an unstable Lisfranc or medial column injury
Surgical Management
Indications

Indications
Multiple metatarsal fractures and an unstable medial column or Lisfranc injury are the
most common indications for surgical management. Closed reduction and percutaneous
pinning of metatarsal fractures is most common, with formal open reduction and
internal fixation reserved for patients with comminuted fractures from higher-energy
mechanisms of injury and children nearing skeletal maturity. Lisfranc fracture
dislocations are best managed via open reduction and internal fixation.
Fifth Metatarsal Fractures and Iselin Disease
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Chronic versus acute-on-chronic pain at the base of the fifth metatarsal differentiates avulsion
fractures from apophysitis.

Patient History
Iselin disease was first described in 1912 as a traction apophysitis at the base of the fifth
metatarsal caused by the peroneus brevis. Thought to be a stress reaction at the
apophysis with microfractures around the insertional Sharpey fibers of the tendon, Iselin

9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Foot and Ankle Sports Injuries in Pediatric Patients
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002083
11/34

disease is similar to Osgood-Schlatter disease of the knee. Iselin disease typically
manifests during periods of rapid growth in children active in repetitive sports activity.
The typical presentation is between 8 and 12 years old in girls and 10 and 13 years old in
boys. Fusion of the fifth metatarsal apophysis is complete by age 18 years8 (Resource 4).
Multiple types of fifth metatarsal base fractures occur in children (Table 1). Pseudo-Jones
(intra-articular) fractures are the most common fractures of the base of the fifth
metatarsal in children and should be considered with any inversion ankle injury.
Distinguishing between fracture types is important because of the watershed blood
supply and higher complication rate associated with Jones fractures, especially in
children nearing skeletal maturity.
Physical Examination
Focal tenderness over the base of the fifth metatarsal and pain with eversion

Physical Examination
Iselin disease manifests as focal tenderness to palpation, swelling at the base of the fifth
metatarsal, and lateral foot pain with weight bearing. It may manifest in an acute, acute-
on-chronic, or chronic fashion. Active resisted eversion and passive dorsiflexion or
plantar flexion with inversion may increase the pain.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard three radiographic views of the foot

Radiography

Standard three radiographic views of the foot are warranted for evaluation. The
apophysis is observed far laterally (parallel to the shaft), located on the base of the fifth
metatarsal, rather than the transverse fracture pattern (perpendicular to the shaft)
observed in patients with a Jones or avulsion fracture.
Classification
Skeletally immature
Skeletally mature
Lawrence and Botte classification sytem9
Zone 1: tuberosity, peroneal avulsion (pseudo-Jones or dancer fracture)
Zone 2: metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction (Jones fracture)
Zone 3: diaphyseal fracture within 1.5 cm of the tuberosity
Differential Diagnosis
Patient history and contralateral foot radiographs may improve diagnosis.

Differential Diagnosis
Acute fracture or avulsion can be differentiated from os vesalianum based on patient
presentation and radiographs. Contralateral radiographs may be helpful in these
situations.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Most fifth metatarsal fractures and Iselin disease


Nonsurgical Management
The mainstay of management includes rest, immobilization, and anti-inflammatory
medications. A short leg walking cast or a controlled ankle motion boot can be used for a
short time. After pain with weight bearing resolves, physical therapy and home exercises
focusing on ankle stretching and strengthening should be initiated.
Outcomes
Pain may last several months to years in patients with Iselin disease but will resolve after
ossification is complete.
Surgical Management
Indications
Adult pattern fractures in skeletally mature patients, nonunions
Skeletally mature patients with delayed healing or nonunion of Jones fracture
No evidence currently supports early surgical treatment in skeletally immature patients.
Kohler Disease
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
4- to 9-year-old boys with chronic medial foot pain

Patient History
Kohler disease (or syndrome) is an osteochondrosis of the tarsal navicular. It typically
occurs in children aged 4 to 9 years, with a higher prevalence in boys (Figure 5). It is

not always symptomatic. It may be an incidental finding observed on radiographs.

Physical Examination
Pain with weight bearing and with palpation over the navicular

Physical Examination

Focal tenderness to palpation, swelling and erythema over the tarsal navicular and the
medial midfoot, and pain with weight bearing may be observed. The characteristic limp
consists of the child-bearing weight on the lateral border of the affected foot, avoiding
medial column weight bearing.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard three-view radiographs of the foot; may obtain navicular view

Radiography
Standard three-view radiographs of the foot are useful for workup. Fragmentation,
sclerosis, and narrowing and flattening of the tarsal navicular bone may be observed.
Contralateral radiographs may help confirm the diagnosis.
Differential Diagnosis
Age-based differential diagnosis because navicular injuries are uncommon

Differential Diagnosis
Stress fracture of the tarsal navicular can be differentiated via bilateral radiographic
findings or patient history and physical examination.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications

Mainstay of management; expect deformity of navicular that does not result in any long-term
functional problems

Management
Rest, immobilization, and anti-inflammatory medication are used for management. A
short period of rest in a short leg walking cast may be necessary in severe cases. The
pain course may be prolonged; however, Kohler disease resolves without long-term
sequelae in most patients. A smaller percentage of patients may have chronic
deformation of the tarsal navicular only observed on radiographs.
Accessory Navicular or Os Navicularis
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Medial foot pain in young athletes (especially in dance, soccer, and martial arts) with
progressive medial bump growth10 (Resource 5)

Patient History
Symptoms of an accessory navicular manifest in an older age group than Kohler disease
and typically are observed in preteen to teenaged patients because accessory navicular
ossification does not occur until age 9 years. The prevalence of an accessory navicular is
as high as 12%, with one-half of accessory naviculars fusing to the navicular. Only a small
percentage of patients will have symptoms. Patients with flat feet have an increased
incidence of accessory navicular symptoms because the insertion of the major portion of
the tibialis posterior occurs on this bone. Displacement of the tendon may result in
valgus deviation of the foot.

Physical Examination
Palpation over the navicular, pain with resisted inversion

Physical Examination
Observation of the foot during weight bearing may reveal pes planovalgus, which may be
associated with accessory navicular symptoms. Focal tenderness to palpation, swelling
and erythema over the tarsal navicular and the medial midfoot, and pain with weight
bearing may occur. The characteristic limp consists of a child-bearing weight on the
lateral border of the affected foot, avoiding medial column weight bearing. Pain with
passive eversion or active inversion may reproduce symptoms.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Navicular view to classify
Geist classification system
Type 1: 2 to 3 mm of sesamoid bone embedded within the distal posterior tibial tendon
without cartilaginous connection to the navicular tuberosity
Type 2: triangular or heart shaped, connected to the navicular tuberosity by 1 to 2 mm of
cartilage, eventual osseous fusion may occur, most commonly has associated with symptoms
Type 3: especially prominent navicular tuberosity

Radiography
Standard three-view radiographs of the foot are warranted for workup. A navicular
radiograph will show the accessory navicular if it is not obvious on routine radiographs.
A navicular view is obtained with the foot positioned plantarly on the image intensifier.
The foot is medially rotated until the plantar surface of the foot is angled 45° to the
image receptor.

Computed Tomography
Rarely indicated
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Rarely indicated
Differential Diagnosis
Stress fracture of the tarsal navicular is differentiated via bilateral radiographic findings or a
patient history of pain. MRI may be warranted in this situation to differentiate the etiology of
pain.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Exhaust nonsurgical treatment options before resection.

Nonsurgical Management
Rest, immobilization, pressure off-loading via doughnut pads, and anti-inflammatory
medications are the mainstay of nonsurgical management. Shoe inserts or orthotics also
may be considered in patients with pes planovalgus. A short period of rest in a short leg
walking cast may be necessary for severe cases. Physical therapy may be useful if an
associated contracture of the heel cords is present.
Surgical Management
Posterior tibialis tendon splitting excision with tendon repair
Accessory navicular excision with posterior tibial tendon advancement (Kidner procedure)


Surgical Management
Excision of the accessory navicular may be offered in chronic, severe cases. Care should
be taken with manipulation of the insertion of the tibialis posterior tendon, and repair
should be performed if required. Postoperative protection of the tendon in a non–
weight-bearing cast is routine.
The Kidner procedure may be considered, particularly in patients with associated pes
planus. The insertion of the posterior tibialis tendon is elevated off the navicular and
plantar advancements performed after accessory navicular excision.11,12
Ankle Sprains Versus Salter-Harris Type I Lateral Ankle Injuries
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History7
Common inversion injury in pediatric patients

Patient History
Low-energy lateral ankle injuries are extremely common in pediatric patients. Inversion
injuries while playing sports account for most of these injuries. Presentation may be
delayed because of delayed development of symptoms, such as swelling, ecchymosis,
stiffness, and limping.
Physical Examination
The location of pain via direct palpation over the lateral ankle ligaments versus the distal
fibular physis determines the diagnosis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Foot and Ankle Sports Injuries in Pediatric Patients
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002083
20/34


Physical Examination
Isolated lateral ankle pain, swelling, and ecchymosis occur. A complete palpation
examination, including the distal tibial physis and plafond, tip of the lateral malleolus,
anterior talofibular ligament, calcaneofibular ligament, fifth metatarsal base, peroneal
tendons, and posterior ankle, should be completed. Ottawa ankle rules are consistent in
adult populations but are not associated with the same sensitivity and specificity in the
pediatric population.
Neurovascular Examination
Perform a standard neurovascular examination.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Three-view radiographs of ankle

Radiography
Standard three-view radiographs of the ankle are warranted. In an acute setting, supine,
non–weight-bearing radiographs are standard of care. Stress radiographs are rarely
indicated in this patient population unless substantial medial deltoid ligament injuries
are suspected.
Differential Diagnosis
Physical examination of the location of tenderness defines the diagnosis.
MRI evaluations show that ankle sprains are much more common than Salter-Harris type I
distal fibula fractures.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM


Differential Diagnosis
Differentiating an ankle sprain from a Salter-Harris type I fracture of the distal fibula is
based on clinical examination because radiographs are normal in both cases. MRIs have
shown that most low-energy lateral ankle injuries in pediatric patients are ankle sprains
without involvement of the distal fibula physis. Extremely rare case reports of late
displacement, infection, or chronic pain were reported in a survey of the Pediatric
Orthopaedic Society of North America membership; however, given the rarity of these
complications and the more common complications associated with cast immobilization,
aggressive management of low-energy lateral ankle injuries via cast immobilization may
not be warranted.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Symptom management and reinjury prevention are mainstays of nonsurgical management.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is the mainstay for low-energy lateral ankle injuries, regardless
whether they are ankle sprains or Salter-Harris type I distal fibula fractures. Initially, a
survey of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America membership showed no
consensus existed with regard to management other than some sort of immobilization,
protected weight bearing until comfortable for as long as 4 weeks, and removal from
sports activity for 4 to 8 weeks. More recently, a level I randomized controlled trial
showed that controlled ankle motion boot immobilization resulted in higher satisfaction
scores, improved range of motion, and lower complication rates than short leg cast
immobilization, making controlled ankle motion boots the preferred treatment option
over short leg casts.

Complications
Pain
Instability

Complications
Reflex sympathetic dystrophy or complex regional pain syndrome is more common in
girls (as much as 84% of the population), with onset within 1 year postinjury.7,13 Prompt
recognition and management via mobilization; physical therapy; psychological
counseling; and possible advanced pain techniques, such as sympathetic blockade,
should be used. Despite aggressive treatment, many patients continued to experience
symptoms 3 years postinjury.
Recurrent instability is common after ankle sprains, particularly in girls, patients engaged
in twisting or pivoting sports activity, and youth athletes. Proper management via a
home exercise program and/or physical therapy addressing lower extremity weakness
and proprioception should be discussed and offered to patients with these injuries.
Rehabilitation
Assessment of sports goals and the risk of recurrence determine the need for physical
therapy.

Rehabilitation
Assessment of patients’ athletic goals and timeline should be discussed at the time of
injury diagnosis. A home exercise program or formal physical therapy (with a physical
therapist or a certified athletic trainer) can be pursued based on team-based decision-
making with the patient and family. Home exercises and physical therapy focused on

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002083
23/34

propioceptive and balance training are most effective in preventing recurrent lateral
ankle injury.14
Surgical Management
Lateral ankle ligament reconstruction or imbrications can be performed; however, limited
outcomes evidence is reported in the literature.

Surgical Management
Lateral ankle ligament imbrication or advancement (eg, Brostrom type procedure) and
lateral ankle ligament reconstruction (eg, Chrisman-Snook type procedure) have been
reported.15 Numerous techniques can be performed; however, comparative outcomes
studies are limited.
Peroneal Tendon Instability
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Inversion or direct blow injury with snapping of the lateral tendons

Patient History
Peroneal instability in pediatric patients is rare, occurring in only 0.3% to 0.5% of those
with ankle instability. The peroneus brevis and longus tendons are contained within the
retrofibular groove and the superior peroneal retinaculum. Congenital flattening of the
groove, ligamentous laxity, and traumatic tears of the superior peroneal retinaculum
(such as after an ankle inversion injury) may lead to peroneal instability symptoms.

Physical Examination
Instability may be difficult to reproduce because of guarding and fear or anxiety.

Physical Examination
Posterolateral ankle pain, sensations of instability, and palpable snapping or subluxation
of the tendons can be observed on physical examination.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard three-view radiographs of the ankle are warranted for initial workup.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI can be used to evaluate fibular groove depth, injury to peroneal tendons, the location of
the peroneal muscle belly, the quality of superior peroneal retinaculum, and soft-tissue
masses within the groove.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
A minimum of 6 weeks of nonsurgical treatment is warranted in patients with an acute, first-
time dislocation or subluxation. Cast immobilization, limited weight bearing, and physical
therapy may be attempted.
Contraindications
Nonsurgical treatment often fails in patients with chronic, recurrent peroneal subluxations,
and surgical treatment should be considered.

Indications
Chronic, recurrent peroneal subluxations in patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails.
Techniques and Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Assessment of physeal status and growth remaining at the distal fibula influences surgical
planning. Groove deepening procedures should be avoided in patients with open distal fibula
physes. Calcaneofibular ligament transfer has been successful in skeletally immature patients
with chronic peroneal tendon instability.
Outcomes
Stenquist et al13 reported low recurrence rates (5.5%), stiffness as a major complication (22%)
and improved patient-reported outcomes at 2-year follow-up of patients with a mean age of
15 years who underwent calcaneofibular ligament transfer for the management of recurrent
peroneal tendon instability (Resource 6).
Freiberg Infraction (Osteochondrosis of the Second Metatarsal
Head)
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History(Resource 7)16
Chronic pain at the second metatarsal head

Patient History
Chronic pain of the second metatarsal head often occurs after minor, acute trauma.
Mechanical symptoms and limited metatarsophalangeal range of motion may be late
symptoms. Highest prevalence is in female adolescents during rapid growth.

Focal tenderness of the second metatarsal head and painful second metatarsophalangeal


Physical Examination
Focal tenderness to palpation of the second metatarsal head and painful second
metatarsophalangeal range of motion, crepitus or mechanical symptoms may occur late.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard three-view radiographs of the foot are warranted for initial workup.
Staging16
Stage 1—A fissure develops in the ischemic epiphysis. This fracture may be so narrow that little
more than a knife blade may be inserted. The opposing cancellous bone on either side of the
fissure appears sclerotic.
Stage 2—Central resorption of bone within the metatarsal head results in the subchondral bone
subsiding. The hyaline cartilage overlying this area hinges at the periphery of the defect, which
results in alteration of the articular surface.
Stage 3—Continued resorption allows the subchondral bone to sink further centrally into the
head, creating peripheral irregularities of the intact joint surface. These projections may fracture
but maintain their attachments to the surrounding soft tissues. During this phase, an isthmus of
the articular cartilage on the plantar aspect of the metatarsal head remains intact.
Stage 4—Fractures of the peripheral projections and the plantar isthmus of articular cartilage are
present. Continuity of the articular surface is disrupted, and the subsided central portion of the
articular surface becomes an osteochondral loose body. The epiphysis is likely closed at this
stage.

Pediatric Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Talus
Overview
Osteocohondritis dissecans (OCD) of the talus is relatively rare in pediatric patients.
True incidence unknown and often found incidentally on routine, trauma-related
radiographs (eg, ankle inversion injury)
Medial talus OCD lesion may result from an acute ankle inversion injury
Lateral talus OCD lesion may result from compression from the fibula
Imaging Studies
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Useful evaluation of cartilage integrity and characterization of lesion size and depth

Stable lesions show no radiographic or MRI characteristics of loose body formation or
chondral degradation.
May show edema within the subchondral bone bed with intact overlying articular cartilage
Unstable lesions may show synovial fluid tracks, subchondral cysts, or associated loose body.
Management
Few studies in skeletally immature patients
Arthroscopy or open arthrotomy can be used for lesion exposure or access, depending on
surgeon skill and experience, OCD size and location, and surgical plan
Stable lesions
OCD drilling
Antegrade (transtibial) or retrograde (transtalar) techniques can be used.
Antegrade drilling
Simple approach with direct visualization of the articular side of the lesion
Care must be taken to limit drill passes across the distal tibial physis and to limit overlying
articular cartilage injury to the distal tibia and talus.
Retrograde drilling
More technically demanding
Preserves overlying talus articular cartilage
May be accomplished with the use of arthroscopic guides and intraoperative fluoroscopy18-
20
Unstable lesions
Lesion débridement, marrow stimulation, and fragment fixation
Good outcomes in small case series21,22
Special considerations in skeletally immature patients
Surgically accessing large lesions is a challenge in pediatric patients given the size of the
ankle joint and the location of the distal tibial physis.
Avoid medial malleolus osteotomy in patients with substantial distal tibia physis growth
remaining.
Advanced techniques using biologics, osteochondral allografts, or osteochondral autografts
have not been reported in patients who are skeletally immature.
Outcomes
Edmonds et al23 showed that one in four children who underwent surgical management of
symptomatic osteochondral lesions of the talus had advancing Kellgren-Lawrence scores
